source.title: A short survey on almost orthogonal vectors in a few specific large dimensions

record.file_problem: None; the full survey text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The survey discusses superposition as context and reports its own embedding-geometry measurements and vector-generation simulations, but it does not test sparse-feature storage, capacity competition, SAE features, or the dimensionality of superposed features.
record.gate_note: The authors cite Toy Models of Superposition and describe the idea that language models may encode concepts as nearly orthogonal directions. Their own measurements are pairwise cosine statistics of context-free token input embeddings, not measurements of features or superposition. The simulations generate arbitrary vector collections, not feature-bearing networks; they therefore do not test the versions. The survey also reports simulation results in figures and Table 7, but these do not establish any of the listed version claims.
record.test_reason: A math survey on how many almost-orthogonal vectors fit in R^n. Its own empirical parts do not test any version. Pairwise cosine statistics of context-free token input embeddings are not feature directions or neuron polysemanticity. The vector-generation simulations use arbitrary vector sets, not trained networks with sparse features. Superposition (Elhage et al.) is cited only as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that existing theoretical bounds are far from practical results, and that R^768 can hold an order of magnitude more 0.1-almost-orthogonal vectors than basis vectors. They describe this as 'a lot of space' for lossily storing information as directions. They also note that input-embedding cosine similarities are mostly positive. They make no empirical claim that models actually use superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The study surveys mathematical bounds and generates vector collections; it does not implement or evaluate the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Embedding cosine distributions differ substantially across the listed models.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 13 encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder models, mean pairwise cosine similarity of token input embeddings is positive. It ranges from 0.0234 (roberta-base) to 0.5283 (distilbert). Normalized distributions look close to Gaussian.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Token input embeddings of transformer language models are anisotropic, with predominantly positive pairwise cosine similarity rather than near-orthogonality.

fits_no_version.finding: Simulations (random sampling, JL projection, energy minimization) fit far more vectors than dimensions at small max |cos|. Example: 8000 vectors in R^768 with max |cos| 0.0823 (Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometric capacity: in dimensions 512–2048, an order of magnitude more directions than the dimension fit at a cosine threshold of about 0.1.

record.problems: The paper is a survey, and its AI-related empirical measurements cover only context-free input embeddings, not contextual activations or feature representations. The embedding cosine distributions are presented graphically, while Table 4 gives summary statistics; the study does not test whether the measured vectors correspond to semantic features.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Simulation results in Figures 8–17 and Table 7 concern generated arbitrary vector collections, not feature-bearing networks, and do not test any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No trained toy networks, sparse features, sparsity-dependent transition or feature geometry. The simulations only count how many generated vectors fit under a cosine threshold (Table 7).
No neurons, polysemanticity or allocation of capacity by feature importance.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity examined.
Only token input-embedding cosine statistics. No feature spread across neurons and no dictionary/SAE recovery.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly unlinked (versions none, cannot_determine). Table 7 simulation results are reasonably left out, since they concern arbitrary vectors, not models. They could be noted as a geometric-capacity finding (added to fits_no_version). The record's 'nearly orthogonal' proposed claim is fine as an anisotropy claim.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sparse features, overcomplete feature storage in a network, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular feature geometry.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity, limited-capacity competition, or allocation of dimensions by feature importance.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Measures token input-embedding similarities, not feature spread across neurons or recovery of sparse features with a dictionary or SAE.
Does not evaluate whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
Does not measure the dimensionality of model features or whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions.
